games.fanatic_story:
Teresa Ocampo already did her Thanksgiving good deed in the Red Zone at SoFi Stadium. On November 18 she waved cars through the Hollywood Park and Rams turkey drive, the one that fed the first 2,500 cars, and she still swears Quentin Lake handed a frozen bird through a minivan window like it was a fourth-down snap.

Gus Lindqvist flew in from De Pere with a carry-on full of cheese curds and a grievance about the weather. Back home, Titletown had to rebuild the skating ice on Hy-Vee Plaza last weekend because it got too warm. Too warm. In Green Bay. In late November.

Gus: The ice outside Lambeau melted, and I still flew somewhere it's going to be seventy-two degrees at kickoff. My brother-in-law has already made a meme about it.

Teresa: Wear the sunglasses you pretend you don't own. Nobody here will tell.

So here's the night before Thanksgiving in Inglewood. Two teams with matching records, six wins and four losses apiece, and both coming off last Sunday on the couch. Ten days to stew is a long time for a football fan, and the two of them stewed in opposite directions.

Gus spent his ten days on Minnesota. The last thing his Packers did was get shoved around at Lambeau by the Vikings, a loss so ugly he took the long way home so the neighbors wouldn't see his face. Teresa spent hers in a parade of highlights. The Rams have won four straight: in Las Vegas, against the Chargers, in Washington, and then a beatdown in Arizona she replays on her phone at red lights.

Teresa: Four in a row. Kyren Williams runs like he's late for dinner.

Gus: Christian Watson has nine hundred and sixteen receiving yards. Look it up. Seven touchdowns. He runs past people the way my uncle runs past a salad.

That one stings, because it's true. Watson has been the reason Jordan Love can throw it deep without blinking. Love has twenty touchdown throws and only seven interceptions, and Gus treats that interception count the way some people treat a family heirloom. He won't let anyone touch it.

Teresa's counter is Matthew Stafford, who has nineteen touchdown throws, and the Rams defense, which has given up fewer points than the Packers have. She also has Byron Young, who keeps showing up in the backfield like he got a calendar invite.

Gus: Lukas Van Ness has six sacks. Evan Williams has eighty-four tackles. We tackle in Green Bay. It's a cultural thing.

Teresa: You also got run off your own field by Minnesota.

Gus: We don't talk about the Vikings at the dinner table, Teresa. That's a family rule.

Here's what neither of them says out loud. The Rams have been better on the road than at SoFi this season, and that bugs Teresa more than she admits. She calls the place a palace and the screen is enormous, but the crowd at SoFi has seen two wins in four tries this year. Gus knows the Packers have taken care of business away from Lambeau, winning three of five, including a big day in New England.

So the night comes down to a simple question. Can Love and Watson get loose against a defense that hasn't let anybody get loose for a month? Or does Stafford get the early lead, hand it to Williams, and let the crowd do the rest while everybody's thinking about pie?

Teresa's plan is to be home by ten, brine the turkey at midnight, and wake up thankful. Gus's plan is to sleep on her couch and insist the cheese curds count as a side dish.

Gus: If we win, I'm telling everybody back home it was colder here than Green Bay.

Teresa: It's seventy-two degrees.

Gus: In my heart, it's a frozen tundra.

My call: Rams 26, Packers 20.

Darnell Whitfield has staked out the same curb on Woodward Avenue since he was nine, and this Thursday the curb is part of history. America's Thanksgiving Parade steps off at 8:45 in the morning for the 100th time, with Dan Gilbert as grand marshal, 33 floats, five giant balloons and a brand-new Big Head of Jeff Daniels bobbing down the street like it owns the place.

Kasia Nowicki drove in from Berwyn on Wednesday night with a thermos of coffee, a folding chair and a Bears stocking cap she refuses to take off indoors.

Kasia: A hundred parades. Do you know how many times you've told me about the World War Two years?

Darnell: Twice a year. They skipped it in 1943 and 1944, which is why number one hundred lands now and not two years ago. History matters, Kasia.

Kasia: So does the fourth quarter.

Darnell will walk from the end of the parade route at Congress Street straight to Ford Field, the way his dad did, and Kasia will follow him because she has nowhere else to stand. That's the Detroit Thanksgiving: balloons in the morning, football by one, and somebody's aunt texting about the gravy the whole time.

This one is the real thing, too. These two have the same record, eight wins and two losses, and the winner sits alone on top of the division going into December. Both teams played Sunday. Nobody is fresh, and nobody cares.

Darnell's case starts at home. The Lions haven't lost at Ford Field all season. Five games there, five wins, and six for six at home if you count the trip to Munich that went down as a home date, and Darnell absolutely counts it. Jahmyr Gibbs has 1,098 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns, and Darnell describes every one of them by pointing at the sky and saying "gone."

Darnell: Gibbs touches the ball in space and the whole building stands up at once. You can feel it in the concrete.

Kasia: Caleb Williams can make the whole building sit back down.

She means it. Williams has been sharp when it counts. The Bears have won five in a row, and the run started with a road win in Atlanta and hasn't stopped. D'Andre Swift has 10 rushing touchdowns, Luther Burden III has turned into the guy Williams looks for on third down, and Jeffery Simmons leads the defense in sacks.

Darnell counters with Amon-Ra St. Brown, who has eight touchdown catches and the best hands in the state, and Jared Goff, who has thrown 20 touchdowns with only four interceptions. Darnell has the interception count tattooed on his memory. He brings it up the way other people bring up the weather.

Kasia: You know what I remember? Week Two. We lost to Minnesota and I didn't speak to anyone for a day. Then we figured it out. We're tougher now.

Darnell: You were tougher in Seattle. Thursday you're at Ford Field with a hundred parades worth of noise in the building.

Kasia doesn't love that part. Both teams have scored plenty this fall, and both defenses have had a few long Sundays. She's convinced this turns into a slugfest instead of a shootout, because division games on short weeks always end up with somebody bleeding on the turf in the fourth quarter. Darnell thinks Gibbs gets loose once, maybe twice, and that's all it takes.

The plan is simple. Parade at 8:45, stuffing at the half, family arguments after. Darnell brought an extra Honolulu blue scarf for Kasia in case she wants to switch sides by the second quarter.

Kasia: I'd rather walk home to Berwyn.

Darnell: That's a long walk. You'll miss pie.

Kasia: I'll take my chances.

When the last balloon drifts past Congress and the stadium fills up, Darnell expects Detroit to do what it has done at home all season. Kasia expects to sweat out every snap until the clock hits zero, and in a game this close, she probably will.

My call: Lions 27, Bears 24.

games.fanatic_story:
Rhonda Castillo has watched every Cowboys Thanksgiving halftime show since Reba McEntire opened the whole tradition at Texas Stadium in 1997, and she has opinions about all thirty of them. This year's headliner for the Salvation Army Red Kettle Kickoff is Miranda Lambert, raised in East Texas about an hour from Dallas, and Rhonda has decided that a hometown girl on the halftime stage is a sign.

Vinnie Scarpa flew down from South Philadelphia on Tuesday night, mostly to argue with her in person. He brought a soft pretzel in his jacket pocket for luck. It's been in there since the airport.

Vinnie: You think a country singer decides a football game?

Rhonda: I think a Texas girl at halftime in Arlington on Thanksgiving doesn't happen by accident. Also, we beat you by seventeen in your own building last month.

That's the part Vinnie doesn't love. The Cowboys went into Philadelphia in October and ran the Eagles off their own field, and the Eagles then lost two more before they finally found a win. Seven losses in a row, start to finish. Vinnie stopped answering texts from his cousins around Halloween.

Then last Sunday happened. The Eagles beat Pittsburgh by three, Joe Milton III had the ball in his hands, and Vinnie walked out of the Linc like a man who'd been let out of jail.

Vinnie: One win. That's all I needed. Milton's got the strongest arm I've seen in green in years. He throws a deep ball that comes down with snow on it.

Rhonda: He'll be throwing it to Caleb Downs.

She's not wrong to feel good. Dak Prescott has 25 touchdown throws and only six interceptions. CeeDee Lamb has 1,108 receiving yards and nine scores, and Javonte Williams has run for 10 touchdowns. This Dallas team can score from anywhere, and it showed it Sunday by dropping fifty-one on Tennessee.

Vinnie: You also gave up forty-six to San Francisco the week before. Your defense has a revolving door.

Rhonda: Quinnen Williams has eight sacks. Tell Milton to bring a helmet with extra padding.

That's the honest truth about these Cowboys. They are thrilling and maddening in the same afternoon, a team that has scored a ton and given up nearly as much. Rhonda has a rule about Thanksgiving games: never leave the couch until the clock is all zeros, because this team has made her cry in the fourth quarter more than once this year.

Vinnie, for his part, knows the Eagles don't have the firepower to trade touchdowns all day. What they have is Nolan Smith Jr., who has six sacks, and a defense that wants to make this ugly, even with Zack Baun on injured reserve. DeVonta Smith and Saquon Barkley have had quieter years than anybody in Philadelphia expected, and Vinnie would like a word with the football gods about that.

Vinnie: Just keep it close into the fourth. Make Dak earn it. That's our whole plan.

Rhonda: Your whole plan is hoping.

Vinnie: Hoping got us one win. I'll ride it.

Here's what both of them agree on. The red kettles come out at halftime, Miranda Lambert sings, and everybody watching gets asked to give something to people who need it this winter. Rhonda has already put a twenty in the kettle outside her grocery store in Grand Prairie. Vinnie says he'll match it if the Eagles keep it within one score.

Rhonda: That's not how charity works, Vincent.

Vinnie: It's how Philadelphia works.

The turkey will be dry, the arguments will be loud, and the Cowboys will probably need a late stop to put the Eagles away. Rhonda will be on her feet for it. Vinnie will be holding a cold pretzel and praying.

My call: Cowboys 27, Eagles 22.

games.fanatic_story:
Marty Kowalczyk will run eight kilometers through downtown Buffalo on Thursday morning and then sit in a cold seat in Orchard Park for three more hours that night, and he calls that a balanced holiday. The YMCA Turkey Trot turns 131 this year. It's the oldest consecutively run footrace in the world, and for the first time in a generation it has a new course, a single loop that starts and ends at the Buffalo Convention Center and still sends the runners down Delaware Avenue for the back half.

Della Ruiz came in from Overland Park on Tuesday and was informed, at the baggage claim, that she would be running too.

Della: I flew here for football. Nobody said anything about cardio.

Marty: Fourteen thousand people do it every year. Little kids. Grandmothers in turkey hats. You'll be fine. Just don't wear the red jacket, people will think you're lost.

Della: I'm wearing the red jacket to the game, Marty. I'm wearing it to the race. I might wear it to dinner.

This is the game both of them circled in August. The Bills have nine wins and one loss. The Chiefs have eight and two. It's Thanksgiving night, the whole country is full of turkey and watching, and somebody is going to walk out of Highmark Stadium holding the inside track to January.

Marty's whole argument is Josh Allen and the run game nobody in Kansas City wants to talk about. James Cook III has 1,060 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns, and Marty has started calling him "the Fourth of July" because every carry looks like a fireworks show. Greg Rousseau has 10 sacks. The Bills have won six straight since a home loss to New England, and Marty still won't say the word "Patriots" indoors.

Della: Patrick Mahomes has twenty-two touchdown throws and four interceptions. Four. You know how many your guy has thrown?

Marty: We don't count those in Western New York. It's bad luck.

Della's not just talking about Mahomes, though. The Kansas City defense has given up fewer points than Buffalo's has, and Nick Bolton is everywhere. George Karlaftis has eight sacks. Kenneth Walker III gave the Chiefs a ground game Della kept describing as "rude," and she is still sore that a groin injury keeps him out of this one.

Della: We play defense now. Mahomes doesn't have to win it by himself. He just has to win it at the end.

Marty: He's done that to us enough times. You don't have to remind me.

That's the history neither of them wants to say out loud. Marty has been to too many January nights where Mahomes had the ball last. He knows the feeling in his stomach when the clock gets inside two minutes and the red jerseys start celebrating. He's trying very hard to convince himself this year is different, and the record says it might be.

The forecast says the sky might open up Thursday night, and Marty is quietly thrilled. Rain in late November in Orchard Park means a slippery ball, a lot of handoffs and a crowd that refuses to sit down. Della packed a poncho. Marty told her ponchos are for tourists.

Della: I am a tourist.

Marty: Not tonight. Tonight you're a Bills fan who's wearing the wrong jacket.

They'll eat turkey sandwiches in the parking lot at five, argue about Travis Kelce until six, and by kickoff neither of them will be able to feel their legs from the morning run. Marty thinks Allen makes one more throw at the end. Della thinks Mahomes gets the ball with time left, which is the scariest thing in football.

Neither one will be shocked if it comes down to the final snap. That's what these two teams do to each other.

My call: Bills 25, Chiefs 23.

Downtown Pittsburgh is still glowing from last Saturday. Light Up Night turned 65 this year, with Zambelli fireworks above the rivers, bridges lit up and the city's 113th Christmas tree switched on in front of the City-County Building. Dom Petrakis was on Grant Street for all of it, holding his granddaughter on his shoulders and a Terrible Towel in his back pocket, because you never know.

Lorna Haskell landed from Denver on Wednesday and wanted to know why everyone in the airport was already talking about Friday.

Dom: Because it's Black Friday, it's three o'clock, and it's the Steelers at home. Nobody's shopping. The malls are going to be empty and the stadium is going to be shaking.

Lorna: Your team lost its last two.

Dom: We don't lose at home. Four games at Acrisure, four wins. Ask Atlanta. Ask Cincinnati. Ask Indianapolis. Ask Cleveland.

That's the whole Pittsburgh argument, and it's a good one. The Steelers have been a different team in their own building. The trouble is the road. A blowout in Cincinnati and a gut punch in Philadelphia have Dom's neighbors in Carrick calling the radio shows again, and that's never a good sign in this town.

Lorna's Broncos come in on a heater. Denver has won six in a row and beat Las Vegas going away last Sunday. The Broncos lost the opener in Kansas City and a game in San Francisco early on, and since then they've been the team nobody wants to see on the schedule.

Lorna: Alex Singleton has a hundred and eighteen tackles. A hundred and eighteen. He's in on every play like he's paying rent there.

Dom: T.J. Watt doesn't need a hundred tackles. He needs one good one on your quarterback.

Watt has seven and a half sacks, and Dom has a rule: if Watt gets home on the first series, the whole stadium comes alive. Lorna's answer is Bo Nix, who has twelve touchdown throws and only five interceptions and doesn't panic when the pocket caves. Jaylen Waddle gives him somebody fast to look for, and Lorna says Denver will have to run the ball without J.K. Dobbins, who is suspended for this one, when the wind kicks up.

The wind is going to howl. The forecast for Friday afternoon says low forties with gusts past twenty, and Dom has never been happier about a weather report.

Dom: That's Pittsburgh football. Nobody's throwing the ball sixty yards in that. You hand it to Jaylen Warren and you make them tackle him. Seven hundred and forty-seven yards. He runs angry.

Lorna: Our defense eats running backs.

Dom: Your defense never ate in Pittsburgh in November.

Dom still can't get used to the old man in black and gold, and every time Rodgers finds DK Metcalf on a back-shoulder throw, Dom yells like he's been a fan for twenty years. Dom: You'll find out the other way, kid.

Lorna: We'll see who's buying the hot chocolate.

games.fanatic_story:
Andre Fontenot is going to have the longest weekend in the NFL. Saturday at one o'clock he'll be in the Caesars Superdome for the 53rd Bayou Classic, Grambling against Southern, surrounded by two marching bands trying to blow the roof off. Sunday at one o'clock he'll be in Cincinnati in a Saints jacket, still hearing tubas in his sleep.

Corinne Albers has been warned. She's a West Side lifer who has had Bengals season tickets since the old stadium, and she plans to meet Andre at the airport with a sign and a container of chili.

Corinne: You're coming straight from a football game to a football game?

Andre: That's Thanksgiving weekend in New Orleans, baby. The Bayou Classic is church. The Saints are family. You go to both.

Corinne: Friday night we light the tree on Fountain Square. Fireworks at seven-thirty. You're missing it.

Andre: I'll see the pictures. I'm busy watching Southern.

Corinne has the better team and she knows it. The Bengals sit at seven wins and three losses, and Joe Burrow is having one of those seasons where you check the stat sheet twice to make sure you read it right. Twenty-nine touchdown throws. Six interceptions. Ja'Marr Chase has 909 receiving yards and catches everything near him. Boye Mafe has nine and a half sacks, and Corinne talks about him like he's her nephew.

What's bugging her is Monday night. The Bengals lost in Washington by two, on the road, in a game she watched through her fingers, and now they're back home on a short week.

Corinne: We had it. We had it right there. I'm still mad about the last drive.

Andre: You're mad about losing by two? We lost to Chicago by eight and I bought everybody gumbo afterward. Perspective.

That's the Saints season in a sentence. New Orleans has three wins, and Andre still shows up to everything. Tyler Shough has thrown 16 touchdowns and become the guy Andre defends at every family dinner. Chris Olave has 866 receiving yards. Carl Granderson has eight and a half sacks, and Andre says he's the only Saint who looks angry in every photo, which he means as the highest compliment.

The Saints were in Paris this year, too, playing Pittsburgh at the Stade de France, and the Bengals went to Madrid and beat Atlanta at the Bernabéu. Andre brought this up so he could say both teams have seen the world. Corinne brought up that only one of them came home with a win.

Andre: Okay, fine. But I've seen the Eiffel Tower.

Corinne: I've seen Burrow win in the building where Real Madrid plays.

Here's what both of them know. The Bengals score in bunches. They put up 38 on Pittsburgh and 43 on Tennessee and 35 in Baltimore. If Burrow gets Chase loose early, this could be a long afternoon for the visitors. But the Saints have hung around more than people think. They lost by one in Detroit in the opener, they won in Baltimore, they've been in plenty of games late, and Andre's whole plan is to make it ugly enough that it stays close.

Andre: Keep Burrow on the sideline. Run Shough on a bootleg every third down. Make the Bengals sweat.

Corinne: The Bengals don't sweat. The Bengals have Chase.

The chili will be good, the wind will be gusty, and Andre will be running on about four hours of sleep. Corinne will make him stand for every Bengals touchdown because those are the rules in her section. He'll stand. He'll grumble. He'll stand again.

Andre: Next year, you're coming to the Bayou Classic.

Corinne: If we win Sunday, I'll think about it.

My call: Bengals 29, Saints 20.

Hank Ostrowski helped hang the garland on the Soldiers and Sailors Monument once, back when his brother-in-law was with IBEW Local 481, and he still talks about it like he built the thing with his bare hands. On Friday night, Circle of Lights turns 64. The electricians strung 52 strands of garland and 4,784 bulbs this year, and the switch flips a little before seven.

Maria DeLuca came in from Staten Island on the Friday morning flight and got the full tour before she'd put her bag down.

Hank: Fifty-two strands. You know how high that monument is?

Maria: I know how high my blood pressure got watching the Giants tie Washington.

That tie still follows the Giants around like a stray dog. New York has six wins, three losses and that one strange afternoon in Landover where nobody won, and Maria has decided to count it as half a win in public and a full loss in private. She drove to the Meadowlands last week to see them beat Jacksonville, and she says she hasn't stopped smiling since.

Hank's Colts are not smiling. Indianapolis has three wins, and the last trip ended with a beating in Houston that Hank describes only as "the Thursday thing." He had ten days to get past it. He did not get past it.

Hank: Jonathan Taylor. That's my answer to everything. Seven hundred and sixty yards and eight touchdowns, and he's been running behind whatever we've got up front with a smile on his face.

Maria: Cam Skattebo runs like he's mad at the ground.

He does. Skattebo has 530 rushing yards for the Giants and an attitude that matches Maria's exactly. Malik Nabers has 747 receiving yards, and the rookie Arvell Reese has turned into the kind of linebacker who's in on every snap. He leads the team in tackles and has four and a half sacks, and Maria says he's the first Giants defender since the old days she'd want her son to copy.

Hank doesn't love talking about Daniel Jones, and Maria knows it, so she brings him up every eleven minutes. Jones played for her team once. Now he throws for Hank's, and he's thrown thirteen interceptions this season. Hank's position is that Jones is "learning on the job," which is a generous position for a man in his eighth season.

Maria: I loved Danny Dimes. I just love him more when he's wearing your colors.

Hank: That's mean.

Maria: That's Staten Island.

Here's the thing Hank actually likes about Sunday. The Colts have been bad, but they've been close a bunch of times. They lost to Kansas City by three. They lost to Dallas by four. They beat Houston and Miami by two each. Lucas Oil gets loud when this team keeps it tight in the second half, and Hank thinks extra rest, a home crowd and the Monument glowing a mile away are enough to turn this into one of those games.

Hank: The crowd never goes quiet at Lucas Oil. We just get worried at a higher volume.

They'll walk down to the Circle after the game either way, because the lights stay up through January and Hank wants Maria to see it at night. He's promised her the best pork tenderloin sandwich in Indiana if the Colts lose. If the Colts win, she's buying.

Maria: I'm not buying anything in this state.

Hank: Then you better hope your guys hold on.

She thinks they will. He thinks they'll make it close. Both of them think it comes down to the last two minutes.

My call: Giants 23, Colts 22.

games.fanatic_story:
Hard Rock Stadium is getting no rest this weekend. Saturday at noon the Hurricanes close their regular season against Boston College, already booked for the ACC Championship Game. Sunday at one o'clock the Dolphins host the Jets. Yolanda Prieto has tickets to both, a cooler with two days of Cuban sandwiches in it and a husband who has stopped asking questions.

Sal Benedetto flew down from Massapequa on Friday, partly for the Jets and partly because he's had enough of November on Long Island.

Sal: Two games in two days? You're going to sit in the same seat twice?

Yolanda: Different seat. Saturday I'm with the Canes people. Sunday I'm with my people. You'd understand if your team ever gave you a reason to show up twice.

Sal: My team just won in Los Angeles. On the road. Against the Chargers. Look it up.

He's very proud of that one, and he has a right to be. The Jets went across the country last Sunday, beat the Chargers by three and flew home feeling like a real football team for the first time in more than a month. Geno Smith has been the steadiest thing in green all year. He has 15 touchdown throws and three interceptions, and Sal treats that interception number like a winning lottery ticket.

Yolanda's year has been harder, and she won't pretend otherwise. The Dolphins have one win. One. And it came in New Jersey, against these same Jets, in a game she still replays in her head on the drive to work.

Yolanda: We beat you. That's all I need to say. You lost to the worst team in the league, and that's us.

Sal: You can't brag about being the worst team in the league.

Yolanda: I can brag about beating you while I'm doing it.

She's earned that. This has been a season of hard news in Miami Gardens. Malik Willis is out, Miami is on its second quarterback, and the home crowd hasn't seen a win yet. Four games at Hard Rock, four losses. Yolanda still goes, still wears the aqua, still sings along when the fight song comes on, and she's tired of people from New York telling her it's hopeless.

What she does have is Ollie Gordon II, who runs hard and has 608 yards, and Chop Robinson, who keeps getting home with five sacks. Jacob Rodriguez has 93 tackles, and Yolanda says he hits people like they cut him off on the Palmetto.

Sal's answer is David Bailey, who has nine and a half sacks and has been terrorizing quarterbacks all fall. Garrett Wilson has 672 receiving yards. Braelon Allen has run for more than seven hundred, and Sal thinks Allen is the key, because a team that can't stop the run in late November in Florida heat is a team that wilts.

Yolanda: It's going to be seventy-two degrees. That's not heat. That's a nice afternoon.

Sal: That's July in Massapequa.

Here's the honest picture. Neither team is going anywhere this year. The Jets have three wins. The Dolphins have one. But a game like this means something different when you're the fan in the seat. For Sal, it's a chance to win two in a row, which hasn't happened all season. For Yolanda, it's a chance to beat the same team twice and give the home crowd one afternoon worth remembering.

Yolanda: First home win of the year. You'll see.

Sal: You said that four times already.

Yolanda: And the fifth time is the charm.

They'll eat the last of the sandwiches in the parking lot, argue about whose quarterback looks worse, and settle into a game that probably comes down to one possession. Sal will have his green jacket off by the first quarter. Yolanda will have her voice gone by the third.

My call: Jets 22, Dolphins 21.

Terrence Ojo flew up from Decatur on Saturday morning and stepped out of the airport into air that hurt his face.

Terrence: Thirty-seven degrees at kickoff, they said. Nobody said anything about the wind coming off the river at the airport.

Ingrid: The stadium has a roof, Terrence. You'll live.

Terrence: My soul doesn't have a roof.

Terrence: Bijan Robinson has nine hundred and fifty-one rushing yards, and he's been doing it for a team that hasn't given him much help.

Saturday night at six-thirty, a parade of boats strung with lights will drift down the St. Johns River, and Buck Tillman will be on the Northbank with a folding chair and his grandson's hand in his. The Jacksonville Light Boat Parade has been running for more than thirty years, and it ends with fireworks near the Main Street Bridge. Buck has seen most of them. He'll be at the stadium the next afternoon, still smelling like smoke and river air.

Celeste Farris drove down from Murfreesboro on Friday and told him, before she'd said hello, that she wasn't here for boats.

Celeste: I'm here because somebody has to sit in the visitors' section and represent.

Buck: Somebody's going to need a hug by the third quarter.

That's about where these two teams are. The Jaguars have seven wins and a real shot at the division. The Titans have one win, and Celeste is honest about it in a way that's almost heroic. She buys the tickets anyway. She wears the light blue anyway. She'll tell you every detail of the one win, in Indianapolis, like it happened yesterday.

Celeste: Cam Ward is going to be good. I'm not asking you to agree. I'm telling you.

Buck: I agree. Just not this Sunday.

Ward has ten touchdown throws as a young quarterback on a bad team, and Celeste thinks that's more impressive than it sounds, given what's been around him. Tony Pollard has 738 rushing yards and six touchdowns. Jacob Martin has seven and a half sacks. There are pieces. They just haven't fit together yet.

Buck's team has fit together most weeks. Trevor Lawrence has 22 touchdown throws. Parker Washington has turned into his go-to target with 748 receiving yards. The Jaguars' defense has been one of the toughest in football, and Buck rattles off the scores from the win against Philadelphia in London and the blowout of Indianapolis like a man reading a grocery list.

The trouble is last Sunday. Jacksonville went to the Meadowlands and lost to the Giants, and Buck didn't sleep well.

Buck: We didn't play with any juice. That's not who we are.

Celeste: That's exactly who you were on Sunday.

Buck: That's why you're going to see the other version this week.

There's history here from earlier this month. The Jaguars went up to Nashville and handled the Titans comfortably, a game Celeste walked out of early for the first time in her life. She says she went to beat traffic. Buck says she went to cry in the car. Both are probably true.

Celeste: You know what's different this time? Nothing. I just want to see us score in the second half.

Buck: That's the most honest thing a Titans fan has ever said to me.

Here's what makes it more than a mismatch for both of them. Celeste's Titans have lost close ones and blowouts and everything in between, and they still show up. Buck's Jaguars have to prove last Sunday was a blip and not the start of something worse. A sloppy start would have half the stadium nervous. A fast start would have the rest of the afternoon feeling like the boat parade the night before, everyone just enjoying the lights.

Buck: If we get up early, I'm buying you a shrimp basket.

Celeste: If you get up early, I'm leaving at halftime.

Buck: You'll miss the shrimp.

Celeste: I'll survive.

She won't leave. She never does. She'll sit through every snap, cheer every Ward completion like it's a playoff touchdown, and drive home to Tennessee proud that she went. Buck will walk out with his grandson, happy, and probably a little relieved.

My call: Jaguars 30, Titans 17.

games.fanatic_story:
Colleen Sheehan booked her hotel in Hollywood because it looked fun on the website. Then Benny Ishikawa sent her the road closures. The Hollywood Christmas Parade is on Sunday, Hollywood Boulevard between Orange and Highland is shut down all weekend, and Highland, Vine and Sunset close starting at four in the afternoon.

Benny: So you'll be fine getting to the game. Getting back to your hotel is your problem.

Colleen: I'm from Quincy. I've been stuck behind worse.

Benny lives in Torrance and has had Chargers season tickets since the team came up the freeway from San Diego. He's not having a good year. Nobody in powder blue is. The Chargers have one win in ten games, and they haven't won at home at all. Benny has been to all five home losses and stayed until the end of every one, which his wife calls loyalty and his brother calls a cry for help.

Benny: We beat Baltimore. On the road. That happened.

Colleen: That was two weeks ago.

Benny: And it was beautiful.

He's not wrong about the beautiful part. A win is a win when you've only got one. And last Sunday the Chargers scored plenty against the Jets and still lost by three, which Benny swears felt like progress.

Colleen's Patriots are sitting at five and five, and she is mostly at peace with it. Drake Maye broke his right fibula in the Detroit game and is listed out, and Colleen is trying very hard not to talk about it. She'll tell you the Patriots won four of five in one stretch this fall, including a blowout of Las Vegas, and she'll leave out the last two weeks, a home loss to Green Bay and a long afternoon against Detroit in Munich.

Colleen: The Munich thing doesn't count. That was basically a vacation.

Benny: You lost by twenty-five.

Colleen: On vacation.

The Patriots have had two weeks to forget about it, with a bye last weekend, and Colleen thinks the rest is exactly what they needed. Elijah Ponder has seven and a half sacks. Christian Elliss has been everywhere. DeMario Douglas has been the most reliable receiver on the roster.

Benny's case is shorter, and it starts with Justin Herbert getting through the concussion protocol. Omarion Hampton runs hard. Khalil Mack is still out there chasing quarterbacks at an age when most players are coaching high school.

Benny: All we need is one clean game. No turnovers. Herbert gets time. Hampton gets going. That's it.

Colleen: That's a lot of things.

Benny: It's three things.

Colleen: That's three more than you've had at home.

That one hurt, and she knew it. She bought him a churro at the stadium to make up for it, which he accepted without saying thank you.

Both of them expect points. The Chargers' defense has had trouble keeping people out of the end zone, and the Patriots have put up big numbers at times this year. Benny thinks Herbert is due for a big day in his own building. Colleen thinks her team has had too long to sit with the Munich loss to come out flat.

What they agree on is that it'll be close at the end, and that the walk back to the car will be miserable for one of them. Colleen is hoping she can get back to Hollywood before the parade traffic shuts everything down. Benny has offered to drive her, which is generous, and also means she has to listen to his talk-radio station the whole way.

Benny: Win or lose, I'm getting you to the parade.

Colleen: Win or lose, I'm wearing this jersey to the parade.

My call: Patriots 24, Chargers 21.

games.fanatic_story:
The carousel is back at Westlake Park. Priya Lund has been telling everyone in Ballard about it for a week. On Friday the downtown tree goes up in lights at five o'clock with fireworks after, and for the first time since 2019 there's a holiday carousel spinning next to it. Priya was there with her daughter, who rode it four times.

Then on Saturday morning she flew to San Jose, where Gil Navarro picked her up at the airport in a 49ers hoodie and a grin she described as unbearable.

Gil: Nine and one, Priya. Nine and one.

Priya: I heard you the first eleven times.

Gil has had a season. His 49ers have one loss, in Atlanta in October, and they've been perfect at Levi's. They went down to Mexico City last Sunday and beat Minnesota by twenty-five. Brock Purdy has twenty-three touchdown throws and only five interceptions. Christian McCaffrey has eleven rushing touchdowns. George Kittle has been Kittle, which Gil says is the highest compliment there is.

Gil: Fred Warner has ninety-six tackles. The man is everywhere.

Priya: Ernest Jones has ninety-eight.

Gil: Fine.

That's the thing about this rivalry. Every time Gil gets going, Priya has an answer. The Seahawks have six wins and one of the best defenses in the league, giving up fewer points than almost anyone. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has more than twelve hundred receiving yards, and Priya calls him "the best thing that's happened to Seattle since the carousel." Byron Murphy II has five sacks in the middle of that defensive front.

Priya: We lost to you by three. In our building. In October. We remember.

Gil: So do we. Fondly.

That game was the kind that sticks with you. The 49ers won by three in Seattle, and Priya has spent a lot of time since then thinking about what might have been. She thinks this is the game where Seattle gets it back.

The Seahawks have had two weeks to get ready, with the bye last weekend, and they won their last game in Las Vegas with the defense holding the Raiders to thirteen. Priya's worry is the offense. Seattle has had quarterback questions, and she's not going to pretend otherwise.

Priya: Our defense can keep us in any game. The question is whether we can score enough to win one like this.

Gil: That's always the question with you guys.

Priya: Says the man whose team gave up forty to Dallas.

Gil: We won that game.

Priya: You gave up forty.

They are both right. The 49ers have won some shootouts this year, and they've also had days where the defense was ordinary. Gil isn't worried. He thinks Purdy is the best he's ever been, McCaffrey keeps finding the end zone, and the home crowd at Levi's will be as loud as it's been all year.

The forecast has a chance of rain, which Priya considers a good omen. She's from Seattle. Rain is home-field advantage wherever she goes.

Gil: It's not going to rain.

Priya: It's going to rain a little. Just for me.

They'll tailgate in the lot with tri-tip, which Gil insists is the correct food for a 49ers game, and Priya will complain that it's not salmon. She'll eat three helpings anyway. When the game ends, one of them will be insufferable for a week.

Gil thinks the 49ers win a close one, like the last one. Priya thinks the Seahawks win a close one, like they should have the last time. Both of them are expecting a fourth quarter worth staying for.

My call: 49ers 26, Seahawks 22.

Gordie has lived in Parma his whole life and he'll tell you there's nothing like downtown Cleveland the weekend after Thanksgiving.

Luz Carrillo flew in from Henderson that morning. She landed to a cold, gray sky and a text from Gordie that just said "Welcome to real football weather."

Luz: It was warm when I left.

Gordie: You'll be fine. Layers.

Luz: I don't own layers. I live in the desert.

The forecast for Sunday night says rain is likely, with temperatures in the forties and a breeze off the lake, and Gordie couldn't be happier. His Browns are undefeated at home this year, and he credits the weather, the crowd and the general unpleasantness of the place.

Gordie: Teams come here and they don't want to be here. That's the whole secret.

Luz's Raiders are in a rough patch. They opened the season with three straight wins, and she was telling everybody in Henderson that this was finally the year. Then they won once in the next eight games. The last three losses came against San Francisco, Seattle and Denver, and Luz has stopped checking the standings.

Luz: Brock Bowers is the best tight end in football. Maxx Crosby is still Maxx Crosby. Nakobe Dean has a hundred and nineteen tackles.

Gordie: And?

Luz: And we have a young quarterback, and I'm being patient.

Fernando Mendoza started last week in Denver, and Luz likes what she's seen even when the scoreboard doesn't. She thinks Ashton Jeanty is going to break one eventually, and she's been saying that since September.

Gordie's team does things differently. The Browns don't blow anybody out. They win close games, a lot of them, and they win them with defense. Carson Schwesinger has more than a hundred tackles and Gordie talks about him like a nephew. Harold Fannin Jr. has been Deshaun Watson's most reliable target. Quinshon Judkins grinds out yards when everybody in the stadium knows he's getting the ball.

Gordie: We beat Houston by three. We beat Pittsburgh by three. We beat Tennessee by three. We beat Baltimore by three.

Luz: Is that a strategy?

Gordie: It's a lifestyle.

The Browns are coming off a bye, rested and at home in prime time, and Gordie is treating it like a playoff game. Luz is treating it like a trip to see friends, with football attached.

What makes it interesting is that the Raiders can score. They've put up points against good teams even in losses, and the Browns haven't always kept people out of the end zone. Bowers can turn a short catch into a long gain. If the rain holds off, it could turn into the kind of game Gordie's not used to, one where his defense has to make a stop late.

Gordie: If it comes down to the last drive, I'll take my chances in this building.

Luz: That's what everybody says right before something weird happens.

They'll watch from the upper deck, Luz in a borrowed coat that goes down to her knees, Gordie in the same brown stocking cap he's worn since the team came back. Win or lose, they're going back to Public Square after to catch the last light show at eleven.

Luz: You sure it's still running?

Gordie: Every half hour until eleven. I checked.

My call: Browns 24, Raiders 21.

games.fanatic_story:
There's an ice rink on the Hillsborough River right now. Winter Village is up at Curtis Hixon Waterfront Park, put on by the Lightning, and Eddie Valdés took his kids skating there on Saturday. Seventeen dollars a skater with rentals, seventy-five minutes on the ice, and Eddie spent most of it holding onto the wall. He's lived in Ybor City his whole life and has never claimed to be a winter person.

Tamika Rhodes drove down from Gastonia on Sunday, eight hours with one stop for gas, and Eddie made her go skating too.

Tamika: I didn't drive five hundred miles to fall on ice in Florida.

Eddie: You didn't fall.

Tamika: I came close four times.

Monday night is what she came for. Her Panthers have won two straight and sit at five and five, right in the thick of things. Last Sunday they beat Baltimore by two points, and Tamika says her voice still hasn't come all the way back.

Tamika: Bryce Young has eighteen touchdown throws. Chuba Hubbard has nine rushing touchdowns. Tetairoa McMillan catches everything.

Eddie: We beat you by thirty in your own building.

Tamika: That was October. Different team.

It was a long day for Carolina, and Eddie hasn't let her forget it. That was the high point of the Buccaneers' year, a stretch in the middle of the season when they won three of four and looked like themselves. Since then they've lost two straight, to Chicago by three and in Detroit, and Eddie is starting to feel the way he did in September when they lost the first four.

Eddie: Bucky Irving is the best thing about this team. Eight hundred and ninety-three yards. Eight touchdowns. He runs angry.

Tamika: Everybody on your team runs angry. You're three and seven.

Eddie: That's why.

The Bucs have been rough at home this year, with only one win at Raymond James, and that bothers Eddie more than anything. He grew up going to games at the old stadium with his dad. Home is supposed to mean something. Josiah Trotter has ninety tackles in the middle of the defense, and David Walker has five sacks. Eddie thinks the defense can get after Young if the crowd gets loud.

Tamika's defense doesn't have big names, but Princely Umanmielen has been getting home, and Devin Lloyd leads the team in tackles. She thinks the Panthers are better than they've been in years. She's been waiting a long time to say that.

Tamika: We're not the team you beat in October.

Eddie: You keep saying that.

Tamika: Because it keeps being true.

Both of them expect a close one. The Panthers have shown they can score, and the Bucs have shown they can run the ball when they need to. Eddie figures a home crowd on a Monday night gives Tampa Bay just enough to get it done. Tamika figures it'll come down to Young having the ball with a couple of minutes left and a chance to make something happen.

Eddie: If it's close at the end, I'm closing my eyes.

Tamika: You can't close your eyes during Monday Night Football.

Eddie: Watch me.

After the game they're going back to Winter Village. Eddie wants another shot at the rink. Tamika wants one of the hot chocolates she saw on the way in and the right to stand at the wall and watch.

Tamika: I'm not skating again.

Eddie: You'll skate.

My call: Buccaneers 24, Panthers 22.
